summary: This informational RFC defines requirements for IPv6 Customer Edge routers to support DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation, handing delegated prefixes to devices on the LAN. It updates RFC 7084.

plainLanguage.summary: A home router gets a big block of addresses from the internet company and passes smaller blocks to other devices. This sets the rules.

questions: what does a ce router need to do for prefix delegation
what prefix length should a ce router delegate on the lan
subtitle: Rules for home and small-office routers to hand spare IPv6 prefixes on to other routers behind them.

tldr.problem: Service providers often delegate more than a /64 to a CE router, but if the router cannot delegate prefixes on its LAN, the extra space goes unused.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds ten requirements (LPD-1 to LPD-10): CE routers MUST support DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (IA_PD) on the LAN, assign /64 prefixes by default, keep a routing table for delegated prefixes, and not delegate lifetimes beyond those learned on the WAN.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 7084 and sets an industry-common baseline for CE routers. Multi-provider (multi-prefix) networks are out of scope.

today: RFC 9818 is an Informational document that updates RFC 7084, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It supplements the CE router requirements with the LAN prefix delegation rules.

sections.title: Why CE Routers Must Delegate Prefixes
sections.content:
Many service providers assign address blocks larger than /64 to an IPv6 Customer Edge (CE) router, as recommended in RFC 6177. If the router does not support the Identity Association for Prefix Delegation (IA_PD) Prefix Option from RFC 8415 on the LAN, it cannot assign any prefixes beyond its own interfaces, and the larger allocation is of limited use.

Supporting IA_PD on the LAN lets those unused prefixes be distributed into the network. The RFC notes that work by the Stub Networking Auto Configuration (SNAC) Working Group depends on prefixes being properly distributed in the LAN.
sections.plainLanguage: If you get a whole box of numbered stickers but can only use the ones on your own door, the rest are wasted. Sharing them with other rooms makes the box useful.

sections.title: Hierarchical and Flat Models
sections.content:
Two models were proposed for sub-delegation beyond a CE router. Hierarchical prefix delegation has the router sub-delegate prefixes by a set of rules. If more than one router does this, a prefix tree forms, and with no routing protocol to discover the topology the tree can become unbalanced and run out of prefixes.

A flat model provisions the router with the initial prefix and assigns /64 prefixes to every other prefix request arriving on the LAN-facing interface. The default configuration of CE routers is designed to be flat, to support zero-configuration networking.

Networks with more than one provider are out of scope, because a solution would need routing, provisioning and policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Either each helper splits its share again and again, which can leave some helpers with nothing, or one person hands out small equal pieces to everyone. The default is the simple, equal pieces.

sections.title: The End-User Network
sections.content:
The model topology (Figure 1) has a service provider router, connected over the customer Internet connection to an IPv6 CE router. Behind the CE router are IPv6 hosts and another router, which in turn serves more IPv6 hosts. A CE router that follows only RFC 7084 gives configuration information to hosts. This document extends that so prefixes can be addressed and routed to both hosts and routers.

The new requirements are in addition to those in Section 4.3 of RFC 7084.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet company talks to your home router, and the home router talks to computers and to other routers that may have their own computers behind them.

sections.title: Assigning and Tracking Prefixes
sections.content:
The first group of LAN Prefix Delegation requirements says what the router does with the prefixes it holds.

  • LPD-1: MUST support IA_PD prefix assignment (Section 13.3 of RFC 8415) on its LAN interfaces.
  • LPD-2: MUST assign a prefix from the delegated prefix as in L-2 of RFC 7084, and MUST log a system management error if too few prefixes are available.
  • LPD-3: the prefix assigned to a link MUST NOT change without a local policy or topology change.
  • LPD-4: after assigning LAN links, MUST keep the remaining prefixes available to other routers via Prefix Delegation.
  • LPD-5: MUST keep a local routing table updated with leases and next hops. Packets to a delegated prefix MUST be forwarded to it regardless of arrival interface, and the route MUST be removed, and the prefix returned to the pool, when it is released or its valid lifetime expires.
sections.plainLanguage: The router must be able to give out blocks, keep each room's block the same, save leftovers for other routers, and write down where each block went so mail finds the right door.

sections.title: Filtering, Prefix Length and Lifetimes
sections.content:
The second group covers safety and details.

  • LPD-6: by default, filtering MUST allow forwarding of packets whose source address is in a delegated prefix, with reciprocal packets of the same flow, following RFC 6092. This updates WPD-5 of RFC 7084. Packets whose addresses are neither assigned to the LAN nor delegated MUST still be dropped.
  • LPD-7: MUST provision IA_PD prefixes with prefix-length 64 on the LAN unless an administrator configures otherwise, since 64 is what SLAAC supports. Hierarchical delegation may use a shorter length.
  • LPD-8: a router generating a ULA prefix MUST continue to provision available GUA prefixes.
  • LPD-9: when provisioning both ULA and GUA, the GUA SHOULD appear first in the DHCPv6 packets.
  • LPD-10: MUST NOT delegate prefixes with lifetimes longer than the remaining lifetimes of the corresponding WAN prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail from handed-out blocks must be let through, blocks are normally one standard size, the public address is listed before the private one, and a block is never lent for longer than the router itself holds it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document adds no new security considerations beyond those in Section 4 of RFC 8213, Section 22 of RFC 8415 and Section 6 of RFC 6092. It has no IANA actions. It also uses its keywords for establishing industry-common baseline functionality rather than strictly for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is risky here beyond what the older rules already cover.

viz.caption: THE TEN LAN PREFIX DELEGATION REQUIREMENTS

items.label: IA_PD on LAN
items.desc: MUST support prefix assignment on LAN interfaces.

items.label: Assign prefixes
items.desc: MUST assign from the delegated prefix; log an error if short.

items.label: Stable prefixes
items.desc: Link prefix MUST NOT change without policy or topology change.

items.label: Keep the rest
items.desc: MUST keep remaining prefixes available for delegation.

items.label: Routing table
items.desc: MUST track leases and next hops; remove routes on expiry.

items.label: Filtering
items.desc: MUST allow delegated-prefix traffic; drop unassigned.

items.label: Prefix length 64
items.desc: MUST use /64 unless an administrator configures otherwise.

items.label: ULA and GUA
items.desc: MUST continue to provision GUA prefixes with a ULA.

items.label: GUA first
items.desc: GUA SHOULD appear first in the DHCPv6 packets.

items.label: Lifetimes
items.desc: MUST NOT exceed remaining WAN prefix lifetimes.
